chapters.title: Grace and Mercy
chapters.subtitle: Grace is the favour of a generous giver, and mercy is God's loyal, motherly love that will not let go
chapters.trueMeaning: Generous favour and loyal, tender love
chapters.nutshell: We often think of grace as a church word for “God's unearned pardon” and mercy as “not getting the punishment we deserve”. In Hebrew, *chen* is the favour you find in someone's eyes, *chesed* is loyal covenant love and *rachamim* is womb-like compassion. In Greek, *charis* was the everyday word for a benefactor's generous gift and the grateful response it called for.
chapters.bigIdea: Biblical grace is God's generous, faithful love freely given, which creates a relationship and calls for a thankful, faithful response.
skeleton: We usually reduce grace to “unearned pardon” and mercy to “escaping punishment”
Chen and chanan: finding favour in someone's eyes; chinnam means “for free”
Chesed is loyal covenant love; rachum and rachamim come from the word for womb
Greek charis means favour, gift and thanks; charisma is a gift; eleos is mercy
Translators chose “mercy”, “lovingkindness”, “steadfast love” and “favour”, each catching part of the picture
In both Israel and Rome, grace lived in real relationships: kings, masters, kin and benefactors
Jesus and Paul show grace as a free gift that changes the receiver
We live it out by receiving freely, giving freely and answering with thankful loyalty

p: Most Christians learn a neat definition: **grace** is “getting what we do not deserve” and **mercy** is “not getting what we do deserve”. These short sayings are useful, but they make both words sound like legal terms, a judge deciding a sentence. Grace becomes a single moment of pardon, and mercy becomes the absence of punishment.

The Bible's words are warmer and fuller. In Hebrew and in Greek they belong to **relationships**: a king who smiles on a petitioner, a family member who stays loyal, a mother who feels for her child, a generous patron who gives a gift. To understand grace, we have to picture people, faces and gifts, not only a courtroom.

sections.h: Chen and chanan: favour in someone's eyes
p: The Hebrew noun *chen* (חֵן) means **favour, grace, charm**. Its most common setting is an everyday phrase: to “find *chen* in the eyes of” someone. “Noah found favour in the eyes of the LORD” (Genesis 6:8). Jacob, afraid of his brother, hopes “to find favour in the sight of my lord” Esau (Genesis 33:8). Ruth asks to glean “after him in whose sight I shall find favour” (Ruth 2:2). The picture is of a person looking up at someone stronger and seeing a **kind face** turned toward them.

The verb is *chanan* (חָנַן), “to be gracious, to show favour”. The priestly blessing says, “The LORD make his face to shine upon you and **be gracious** to you” (Numbers 6:25). David prays, “**Be gracious** to me, O God, according to your steadfast love” (Psalm 51:1), where many versions say “Have mercy on me”. Grace here is a shining face, God turning toward his people.

From the same root comes *channun* (חַנּוּן), “gracious”, used almost always of God (Exodus 34:6; Psalm 103:8; Jonah 4:2). Many Hebrew names carry it: *Channah* (Hannah, “grace”), *Chananyah* (Hananiah, “the LORD has been gracious”) and *Yochanan* (John, “the LORD has shown grace”).

Lexicons also connect the adverb *chinnam* (חִנָּם), “**for nothing, free of charge, without cause**”, to this root. A Hebrew slave “shall go out free, **for nothing**” (Exodus 21:2), and the psalmist complains of those who “hate me **without cause**” (Psalm 69:4), words Jesus applies to himself (John 15:25). Grace is the favour that comes *chinnam*, gratis, without a price tag.

sections.h: Chesed and rachum: loyal love and a mother's compassion
p: Close to *chen* stands *chesed* (חֶסֶד), one of the richest words in the Hebrew Bible. It means **loyal love, steadfast kindness, covenant faithfulness**: love that keeps its promises and goes beyond what duty requires. When God reveals his name to Moses he is “merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in **steadfast love** and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). Psalm 136 repeats in every verse, “for his **steadfast love** endures forever.”

*Chesed* is shown inside relationships. Ruth's loyalty to Naomi and Boaz is called *chesed* (Ruth 3:10). David asks, “Is there not still anyone of the house of Saul, that I may show the **kindness of God** to him?” and cares for Jonathan's lame son for his friend's sake (2 Samuel 9:3). Through Hosea God says, “I desire **steadfast love** and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6).

The word *rachum* (רַחוּם), “compassionate, merciful”, and the plural noun *rachamim* (רַחֲמִים), “compassion, mercies”, come from the same root as *rechem* (רֶחֶם), “**womb**”. The lexicons agree on this link. God asks, “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her **womb**? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you” (Isaiah 49:15). Biblical mercy is not cool tolerance; it is the deep, physical tenderness of a mother.
> Grace (*chen*) is God's face turned toward us; loyal love (*chesed*) is his promise that he will not turn away; compassion (*rachamim*) is his heart moved like a mother's.

sections.h: The Greek words: charis, charisma, eleos and oiktirmos
p: When Jewish scholars translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek (the Septuagint), they usually rendered *chen* with *charis* (χάρις). In Greek Genesis 6:8, Noah “found *charis*”. In ordinary Greek, *charis* had three sides: the **favour** of a giver, the **gift** itself, and the **thanks** that comes back. Paul can write “**Thanks** be to God” with the same word (1 Corinthians 15:57), and the word *eucharistia* (εὐχαριστία), “thanksgiving”, comes from it.

*Charis* is not only for sinners. Luke says the boy Jesus grew “in **favour** with God and man” (Luke 2:52), using *charis*. So the word means generous delight and goodwill, not only pardon for the guilty. From it comes *charisma* (χάρισμα), “**a gift freely given**”: “the free gift of God is eternal life” (Romans 6:23), and the Spirit's “varieties of gifts” (1 Corinthians 12:4). The verb *charizomai* means to give freely or to forgive (Ephesians 4:32).

For *chesed*, the Septuagint most often chose *eleos* (ἔλεος), “**mercy, pity**”. So when Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6, “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13; 12:7), the Greek *eleos* stands for the Hebrew *chesed*. Mary and Zechariah sing of God's *eleos* toward Israel, “to show the **mercy** promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant” (Luke 1:72). Covenant loyalty is still inside the Greek word.

For *rachamim* the Greek often uses *oiktirmos* (οἰκτιρμός), “compassion, mercies”. Paul appeals to readers “by the **mercies** of God” (Romans 12:1) and calls God “the Father of **mercies**” (2 Corinthians 1:3). The cry of the blind and the sick, “Son of David, **have mercy** on me!” (Mark 10:47), uses *eleeō*, the verb from *eleos*.

No single English word can carry *chesed*. Older English Bibles followed the Greek *eleos* and the Latin *misericordia* and often wrote “mercy”: the King James Version renders Psalm 136, “for his **mercy** endureth for ever.” Early English translators also used “**lovingkindness**”, a word that became famous through the King James Version. Modern versions try again: the ESV and NRSV say “**steadfast love**”, the NIV says “his **love** endures forever.” Each choice is fair, and each captures part of the meaning: mercy, kindness, loyalty, love. Readers lose the sense that it is **one word** binding all of these into covenant faithfulness.

*Chen* has a similar story. The KJV says Noah “found **grace** in the eyes of the LORD”; the NIV and ESV say “found **favor**”. Modern versions choose “favor” because “grace” now sounds like a theological term, while the Hebrew is an ordinary idiom used between people. But then English readers miss that Genesis 6:8 and Ephesians 2:8 stand in one line of words.

The English word “grace” comes from the Latin *gratia*, which, like *charis*, meant favour, gift and thanks. That is why we still “say grace” (give thanks) before meals and why “gratis” means free. In Luke 1:28 the angel greets Mary as *kecharitōmenē*, “one who has been **favoured**”. The Latin Vulgate rendered it *gratia plena*, “**full of grace**”, which shaped centuries of Western prayer; the KJV and most modern versions return to “highly favoured” or “favored one”. Translators here balanced the Greek form against a long tradition.

Sometimes English drops “grace” altogether. In Luke 6:32 Jesus asks, “If you love those who love you, what *charis* is that to you?” The KJV says “what **thank** have ye?”, the NIV “what **credit**”, the ESV “what **benefit**”. All are correct, because *charis* covered favour and return, but the link to Jesus' teaching on grace disappears.

In Israel, *chen* lived in a world of **honour and rank**. A servant or petitioner bowed before a master, a king or a powerful relative and hoped to see favour in his eyes. Esther “won **grace and favour** in his sight” before the Persian king (Esther 2:17), a matter of life and death. Ruth gleaned in a stranger's field, and Boaz's kindness meant food for a widow's household. Grace was a face turned toward the weak.

*Chesed* lived in **family and covenant**. It was the loyalty you owed kin, friends and treaty partners, and the extra kindness that went beyond it: burying a relative, keeping a dead friend's family, protecting a guest. When Jacob asks Joseph to bury him in Canaan, he asks him to “deal **kindly and truly**” with him, *chesed ve'emet* (Genesis 47:29).

In the Greco-Roman world, *charis* lived in the system of **patrons and benefactors**. Rich citizens and rulers gave cities buildings, grain and festivals, and people honoured them with inscriptions and loyalty. A gift was to be given freely, but receiving it created a bond: the receiver owed gratitude, honour and faithfulness. The Roman thinker Seneca described the three Graces dancing in a ring as a picture of a benefit passing from hand to hand and returning to the giver. So when Paul says we are saved “by *charis*… as a gift” (Ephesians 2:8), his first readers heard of a generous Benefactor whose gift is free, yet calls for a grateful, loyal life.

sections.h: Grace and mercy in Jewish prayer
p: Jewish prayer is full of these words. The words of Exodus 34:6–7, which Jewish tradition calls the **Thirteen Attributes of Mercy**, are sung on festivals, in the *Selichot* prayers before the High Holy Days and many times on Yom Kippur. Worshippers come to God trusting that he is *rachum ve-channun*, “compassionate and gracious”.

The daily *Amidah* asks God to “grant knowledge **graciously**” (*chonen*), and its last blessing asks for peace, goodness, blessing, “**grace, loyal love and compassion**” (*chen va-chesed ve-rachamim*). The grace after meals (*Birkat HaMazon*) begins by praising God who feeds the whole world “in his goodness, with grace, with loyal love and with compassion.” In Jewish life, grace is not a doctrine to argue about but a reality to thank God for every day.

sections.h: Jesus and the apostles: grace in context
p: John writes that the Word became flesh, “**full of grace and truth**” (John 1:14), and that “from his fullness we have all received, **grace upon grace**. For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:16–17). Many scholars hear an echo of Exodus 34:6, “abounding in *chesed* and *emet*”. Jesus is the face of the same gracious God who met Moses, not a replacement for him.

Paul's “by grace you have been saved through faith… it is the gift of God, not a result of works” (Ephesians 2:8–9) is followed at once by: “we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus **for good works**” (Ephesians 2:10). In the language of benefaction this makes perfect sense. The gift is utterly free; we cannot buy it. But it is meant to change us and to bind us in loyalty to the Giver. “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matthew 10:8).

Grace is also **strength**. When Paul begged to be freed from his weakness, the Lord answered, “My **grace** is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). And the gifts (*charismata*) of the Spirit are grace given in concrete forms for building up the community (1 Corinthians 12).

Receive grace as a **gift**, not as a wage. You did not earn God's favour, and you cannot lose it by being weak. Then let it work in you as it did in Paul: “by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

Answer grace with **thanks and loyalty**. In the Bible's world, the right response to a generous giver is gratitude, honour and faithfulness. Practise *chesed* in your own relationships: keep promises, stay loyal when it costs you, show kindness that goes beyond duty, and let your compassion be as warm as a mother's.

quiz.q: What is the usual setting of the Hebrew word chen?
options: Finding favour “in the eyes of” someone
quiz.why: Chen usually appears in the idiom “find favour in the eyes of”, as with Noah, Jacob, Ruth and Esther.

quiz.q: The Hebrew word for compassion, rachamim, is related to which word?
quiz.why: Lexicons connect rachum and rachamim to rechem, womb, so mercy pictures a mother's tenderness (Isaiah 49:15).

quiz.q: Which Greek word did the Septuagint usually use for chesed?
quiz.why: Eleos, “mercy”, usually stands for chesed, as in Hosea 6:6 quoted in Matthew 9:13.

quiz.q: In ordinary Greek, charis could mean…
quiz.why: Charis covered the giver's favour, the gift and the thankful response; “thanks be to God” uses the same word.

quiz.q: What does Ephesians 2:10 add straight after “by grace you have been saved”?

That good works do not matter
That we are created in Christ Jesus for good works

chapters.title: Truth and Faithfulness
chapters.subtitle: In Hebrew, truth is something you can lean your weight on: a person or a word that holds firm
chapters.nutshell: We usually think of truth as correct information: statements that match the facts. The Hebrew *emet* comes from the root *aman*, “to be firm, to support”, and means reliability and faithfulness as well as truth. The same root gives *emunah* (faithfulness) and *amen*. The Greek *alētheia* means truth and reality, and in the New Testament it carries this Hebrew sense of faithful truth.
chapters.bigIdea: Biblical truth is not only accurate facts but faithfulness you can rely on, seen above all in God and in Jesus, and lived out in faithful lives.
skeleton: We usually treat truth as correct statements and facts
The root aman pictures firmness: a peg in a sure place, a nurse who carries a child
Emet means truth, reliability and faithfulness, often paired with chesed
Emunah is steady faithfulness, and amen means “surely, it holds”
Greek alētheia means truth and reality; alēthinos means genuine
Translators choose between “truth” and “faithfulness”, and each loses something
In Israel truth belonged to witnesses, gates and covenants; in Greece to philosophy
Jesus is the truth in person, and we “do the truth” by living faithfully

p: When we hear the word **truth**, we usually think of facts: a statement is true if it matches reality. Truth is something you know with your head, and you can test it, prove it, or defend it in an argument. In church, “the truth” often means correct doctrine.

These ideas are not wrong, and the Bible cares deeply about not lying. But the Hebrew Bible starts from a different picture. Truth is first of all **something that holds**: a person, a promise or a word on which you can lean your full weight without it giving way. In the Bible, God is true because he is **faithful**.

sections.h: The root aman: what is firm and carries you
p: The Hebrew root behind truth is *aman* (אמן), “**to be firm, steady, reliable; to support**”. Its everyday uses give us vivid pictures. God says he will fasten his servant “like a **peg in a secure place**” (Isaiah 22:23), a peg driven into a firm wall that will not pull out. Moses complains that he cannot carry Israel “as a **nurse** carries a nursing child” (Numbers 11:12); the word for nurse or foster-parent, *omen*, comes from this root. When Ruth's son is born, Naomi becomes his *omenet*, his nurse (Ruth 4:16). The doorposts of the Temple are called *omnot* (2 Kings 18:16).

So the root holds together **firmness** and **support**: a peg that holds, a pillar that bears weight, a guardian who carries a child safely. In a different verb form, *he'emin* (הֶאֱמִין), it means “to believe, to trust”, literally to lean on someone as firm. “Abram **believed** the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6).

The noun *emet* (אֱמֶת), from this root, means **truth, reliability, faithfulness, sureness**. Sometimes it means true words: “Speak the **truth** to one another” (Zechariah 8:16). Sometimes it means a faithful character: “Lead me in your **truth** and teach me” (Psalm 25:5). Often it means both at once: what God says is true because God himself is faithful. “The sum of your word is **truth**” (Psalm 119:160), and “the LORD is the **true** God” (Jeremiah 10:10).

*Emet* is often paired with *chesed*, “loyal love”. God is “abounding in **steadfast love and faithfulness**”, *chesed ve'emet* (Exodus 34:6). Abraham's servant blesses God, who “has not forsaken his steadfast love and his **faithfulness** toward my master” (Genesis 24:27). The psalmist sings, “Steadfast love and **faithfulness** meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other” (Psalm 85:10). In Hebrew, love and truth are not rivals; they are partners.
> In Hebrew, something is true when you can lean on it and it does not give way. God's truth is God's faithfulness.

From the same root comes *emunah* (אֱמוּנָה), **steadiness, faithfulness**. When Moses held up his hands during the battle, Aaron and Hur supported them, “so his hands were **steady** until the going down of the sun” (Exodus 17:12). The word for steady is *emunah*. It is often translated “faith”, but its first meaning is **faithfulness**: “Great is your **faithfulness**” (Lamentations 3:23); “the righteous shall live by his faith” (Habakkuk 2:4).

The word *amen* (אָמֵן) means “**surely, truly, so be it**”. The people answered the covenant curses and blessings with “Amen” (Deuteronomy 27:15–26), and when Ezra blessed the LORD, all the people answered, “Amen, Amen” (Nehemiah 8:6). Saying amen meant: this is firm; I stand on it. Isaiah even calls God “the God of **amen**” (Isaiah 65:16, usually translated “the God of truth”).

Jewish tradition loves this word. The Talmud explains *amen* as the first letters of *El Melekh Ne'eman*, “God, faithful King” (Talmud Shabbat 119b). Another well-known rabbinic saying is: “The **seal** of the Holy One, blessed be He, is **truth**” (Talmud Shabbat 55a).

sections.h: The Greek words: alētheia, alēthinos and amēn
p: The Greek *alētheia* (ἀλήθεια) means **truth, reality, sincerity**, the way things really are as opposed to appearance or lies. A common explanation links it to *a-* (“not”) and *lēthē* (“forgetting, hiddenness”), giving “what is not hidden”. This is a popular and possible explanation, but scholars debate how much it shaped the everyday meaning. The adjective *alēthēs* (ἀληθής) means “true, truthful”, and *alēthinos* (ἀληθινός) means “**genuine, real**”: Jesus is “the **true** vine” (John 15:1) and “the **true** bread from heaven” (John 6:32), and believers serve “a living and **true** God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

The Septuagint usually translated *emet* with *alētheia*, and in its Greek of Exodus 34:6 God is “rich in mercy and **true**” (*polyeleos kai alēthinos*). So when the New Testament speaks of truth, the Greek word already carries the Hebrew sense of **faithfulness**. In Revelation Jesus is called “Faithful and **True**” (Revelation 19:11) and “the **Amen**, the faithful and true witness” (Revelation 3:14).

The Hebrew *amen* passed straight into Greek as *amēn* (ἀμήν). Jesus used it in a striking way: not only at the end of a prayer but at the **start** of his sayings, “*Amen* I say to you”, and in John's Gospel doubled, “*Amen, amen*”. He was putting the full weight of his own faithfulness behind his words.

English has no single word for *emet*. Translators must choose between “**truth**” and “**faithfulness**”. In Psalm 91:4 the King James Version says, “his **truth** shall be thy shield and buckler”; the ESV says “his **faithfulness** is a shield and buckler.” In Exodus 34:6 the KJV has “abundant in goodness and **truth**”, the NIV “abounding in love and **faithfulness**”. The older versions follow the Greek *alētheia* and the Latin *veritas*; modern versions choose “faithfulness” because a shield made of “truth” sounds like an idea, not a protector. Either way, English readers see only half of a word that means both.

With *amen* the issue is different. The KJV writes Jesus' words as “**Verily**, verily, I say unto thee” (John 3:3), from the Latin *verus*, “true”; the ESV says “**Truly**, truly”, and the NIV “**Very truly** I tell you”. These are clear English, but readers no longer hear that Jesus was saying the Hebrew word *amen* that they say at the end of their own prayers.

In Ephesians 4:15 Paul uses a verb, *alētheuontes* (ἀληθεύοντες), literally “**truthing** in love”. English has no such verb, so versions say “speaking the truth in love”. That is a fair rendering, but the Greek includes being true and acting faithfully, not only speaking correctly.

In Israel, truth belonged to **the gate and the witness**. Judges sat in the city gate, and the law demanded careful investigation: “if it is **true** and certain that such an abomination has been done” (Deuteronomy 17:4). No one could be condemned on one witness; it took two or three (Deuteronomy 19:15). The ninth commandment forbids being a “false witness” (Exodus 20:16). The prophet calls Israel to “render in your **gates** judgments that are true and make for peace” (Zechariah 8:16). Truth was a matter of **keeping faith** with your neighbour in public.

Truth also belonged to **covenant and family**. When Jacob is dying, he asks Joseph to “deal **kindly and truly**” with him, *chesed ve'emet*, by burying him in the land of promise (Genesis 47:29). A true person was one whose word held, like a peg in a firm wall.

In the Greek world, truth became a central question of **philosophy**. Plato taught that true reality lies in unchanging, eternal Forms beyond the changing world of the senses. Aristotle defined it simply: “to say of what is that it is, and of what is not that it is not, is true.” This is truth as **correspondence** between words and reality, and it is valuable. But it is more abstract than the Hebrew picture. When Pilate, a Roman governor, asks Jesus, “What is truth?” (John 18:38), he asks a philosopher's question while the faithful Truth stands in front of him.

sections.h: Jesus and the apostles: truth in a person
p: John says the Word became flesh, “full of **grace and truth**” (John 1:14), and “grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). Many scholars hear Exodus 34:6, *chesed ve'emet*, behind these words. Jesus is the faithful love and reliability of God, in person.

So Jesus can say, “I am the way, and **the truth**, and the life” (John 14:6). He does not only teach true facts; he **is** the one on whom you can lean your whole weight. “If you abide in my word… you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John 8:31–32). Knowing the truth here means living in faithful relationship with him.

John also speaks of “**doing** the truth”: “whoever does what is true comes to the light” (John 3:21), an echo of the Hebrew idiom “to do *emet*” (Genesis 47:29). And he urges, “let us not love in word or talk but in deed and **in truth**” (1 John 3:18). Paul says that all God's promises find their “Yes” in Christ, “that is why it is through him that we utter our **Amen** to God” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

Lean on God's truth as you would lean on a firm pillar. When the Bible says God is true, it means he will **keep his word**. Every “Amen” you say is a small act of trust: this holds, and I stand on it.

Then become a person of *emet*. Let your word be reliable, your promises kept and your witness honest. Speak truth, but do it “in love”, as a faithful friend rather than a debater. Truth in the Bible is not only something we believe; it is a way we **live faithfully** before God and our neighbours.

words.gloss: to be firm, reliable; to support
words.note: The root behind emet, emunah and amen.
words.missed: Few English readers see that “believe”, “faithful”, “truth” and “amen” share one Hebrew root.
words.culture: Pictured by a peg in a firm wall, doorposts, and a nurse who carries a child.

words.note: To lean on someone as firm and reliable.
words.missed: “Believe” can sound like holding an opinion; the Hebrew is trusting your weight to someone.
words.culture: Trust in a covenant partner who has made promises, as God did with Abram.

words.note: True words and a faithful character at once.
words.missed: Versions must choose “truth” or “faithfulness”, so readers see only half of it.
words.culture: Truth in the city-gate court and in covenant loyalty to family and friends.

words.note: Moses' hands were emunah, steady, until sunset.
words.missed: “Faith” often sounds like inner belief only; the Hebrew stresses steady faithfulness.
words.culture: A steady, dependable life, the kind of person you can count on.

words.note: The people's answer: this is firm, we stand on it.
words.missed: Said as a closing word, its strong meaning “this holds” is easily forgotten.
words.culture: The congregation's response in worship, still said in synagogue and church today.

words.note: The Septuagint's usual word for emet.
words.missed: Read only as correct information, it loses the Hebrew sense of faithfulness behind it.
words.culture: In Greek philosophy, the real as opposed to appearance or lies.

words.note: The real thing, not a copy or a fake.
words.missed: “True” in English often means accurate; here it means the genuine one.
words.culture: In a world of many gods and idols, the living and genuine God.

words.gloss: to be true, speak the truth
words.note: Literally “to truth”: being and speaking true.
words.missed: “Speaking the truth” narrows a verb that includes living truly.
words.culture: Paul uses it for a church where members build each other up in love.

words.note: Hebrew amen taken straight into Greek.
words.missed: “Verily” and “truly” hide that Jesus said the Hebrew word amen.
words.culture: Jesus used it at the start of sayings, which was unusual and showed his authority.

words.note: Paired with “true” for Jesus, “Faithful and True”.
words.missed: English readers may not link “faithful” to “faith” and “truth” as Hebrew does.
words.culture: In Greek life, a trustworthy friend, servant or ally who keeps faith.

rows.literal: great in loyal love and firmness / faithfulness
rows.why: The KJV follows the Greek and Latin “truth”; the NIV's “love and faithfulness” shows God's reliability but loses the link to “truth”.

rows.literal: a shield and buckler is his firmness (faithfulness)
rows.common: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler (KJV)
rows.why: Modern versions say “faithfulness” because a shield is a person's dependable protection, not an idea.
The wording is exact, but English readers may hear “correct teaching” where John likely echoes chesed ve'emet, faithful love.

rows.literal: amen, amen, I say to you
rows.common: Verily, verily, I say unto thee (KJV)
rows.why: “Verily” (from Latin verus) and “truly” give clear sense but hide the familiar Hebrew word amen.
English has no verb “to truth”, so translators add “speaking”, which narrows a word that includes living truly.

left.label: Abstract idea of truth
items: Truth is correct information
Truth is known mainly with the mind
Truth is proved by argument
“Amen” is just a way to end a prayer
Love and truth often pull against each other

right.label: Hebrew lens
items: Truth is what holds firm and can be relied on
Truth is known by trusting and living faithfully
Truth is shown by keeping your word
“Amen” means “this is firm; I stand on it”
Loyal love and truth belong together (chesed ve'emet)

verses.text: The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.
Lead me in your truth and teach me, for you are the God of my salvation.
Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other.
They are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.
For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.
I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.
And you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.

keyPoints: The Hebrew root aman means firm and supporting: a peg in a sure place, a nurse carrying a child.
Emet means truth, reliability and faithfulness at the same time; God's truth is his faithfulness.
Emet is often paired with chesed, loyal love (Exodus 34:6): love and truth belong together.
Emunah is steadiness and faithfulness, and amen means “surely, it holds”.
Greek alētheia carries the Hebrew sense in the New Testament; alēthinos means genuine.
Translators must choose “truth” or “faithfulness” for emet, and “verily” or “truly” for amen, so something is always lost.
Jesus is the truth in person, and believers are called to “do the truth” in faithful lives.
reflect: When you say “Amen”, what are you really saying you stand on?
Is there an area of your life where people cannot yet rely on your word? What would emet look like there?
How might speaking the truth “in love” change a difficult conversation you are facing?

quiz.q: What is the basic meaning of the Hebrew root aman?
quiz.why: Aman means firm and supporting, seen in a peg in a sure place (Isaiah 22:23) and a nurse carrying a child (Numbers 11:12).

quiz.q: In Exodus 34:6 emet is paired with which word?
quiz.why: God is “abounding in chesed and emet”, steadfast love and faithfulness.

quiz.q: Why do many modern versions say “his faithfulness” in Psalm 91:4 where the KJV says “his truth”?
options: The Hebrew word is different in modern manuscripts
Because emet also means faithfulness and a shield is a dependable protector
Because the verse is about honesty in court
quiz.why: Emet means both truth and faithfulness; “faithfulness” brings out God's dependable protection.

quiz.q: What Hebrew word stands behind Jesus' “Verily, verily” or “Truly, truly”?
quiz.why: The Greek text has amēn amēn, the Hebrew amen, which Jesus used at the start of his sayings.

quiz.q: Which rabbinic saying is about truth?
options: “The seal of the Holy One is truth”
quiz.why: The Talmud (Shabbat 55a) says, “The seal of the Holy One, blessed be He, is truth.”

terms.def: Hebrew root meaning to be firm, reliable and supporting; behind truth, faith and amen.
Truth, reliability and faithfulness; what holds firm.
“Surely, truly, so be it”: a response that says “this is firm”.
Greek for truth and reality; in the New Testament it carries the sense of emet.
Greek for genuine or real, as in “the true vine”.
“Loyal love and faithfulness”, a common Hebrew pair describing God and faithful people.
